title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache cost model
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Nimbus Health through Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies. Discussed cost model assumptions, latency tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted routing, and next steps to run a small benchmark using Nimbus prompt traces. Action items and pricing follow-up agreed.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-07-22 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Aaron Michaels (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Nimbus), Leila Gomez (ML Engineer), Evan Kim (Infra), Sasha (Procurement)

[00:00] Aaron: hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Aaron from Redwood, i'm the AE working with Nimbus. Maya our solutions engineer is here to do the Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and the prefix / KV cache recommendations.
[00:18] Raj: hey, thanks. quick context, our main goal is to cut inference spend for clinical notes summarization but keep 95th latency under 500ms for interactive UI flows. we average ~120 rps right now with big burstiness during business hours.
[00:34] Maya: got it. quick question on current stack — what model family are you using and how are you hosting?
[00:38] Leila: we're on a fine-tuned Llama-2. We're currently self-hosting on EC2 GPUs, mixed p3 and g5, with simple autoscaling. KV cache is not implemented, no prefix caching, and batching is ad-hoc in our app layer.
[00:55] Aaron: perfect, that's very common. today we'll show how Redwood Optimize recommends batching sizes, when to enable prefix caching vs KV cache, and how those knobs affect cost per 1k tokens and p95 latency. we'll also share a small cost model.
[01:10] Maya: slide: "why batching matters" — the idea is throughput efficiency: larger micro-batches amortize dispatch overhead and kernel launch costs. but you also have to balance service latency. for short interactive prompts aggressive batching can hurt p95.
[01:25] Maya: (aside) and we often see customers mis-guess the batch size because they assume steady load; the optimizer looks at your trace distribution.
[01:33] [01:33] Leila: can you clarify micro-batching vs dynamic batching?
[01:36] Maya: sure, micro-batching is grouping requests within a single worker's queue before executing single forward pass. dynamic continuous batching is runtime-level — it tries to fill batches up to a threshold or time window. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching with configurable latency SLOs.
[01:52] Aaron: quick numbers from our typical benchmarks — for a 3B-ish model and seq len 256: no batching cost per token is baseline, with batching 8x it can drop per-token GPU time by ~3-4x depending on kernel efficiency.
[02:06] Raj: that's substantial. curious about bursts — we have spikes where QPS goes 10x for 2-5 minutes.
[02:12] Maya: we recommend a hybrid approach: normal ops use dynamic batching with a 50ms max wait, then ramp to burst mode where you can burst to dedicated instances or fall back to a cheaper model variant. caching helps a lot for repeated prefixes.
[02:25] [02:25] Evan: what exactly do you mean by caching here — prefix cache vs KV cache? our infra team calls things differently.
[02:30] Maya: good question. two types: prefix cache (also called prefix KV) is caching initial activations/kv pairs for common prefixes — e.g., system prompt or common instruction prefixes — that avoids recomputing first N tokens. KV cache as we say is a more general per-request key/value reuse across sessions. Redwood supports persistent KV caches keyed by prefix signature; it's pluggable. sometimes transcripts use K V cache or KV-cache, transcription might show it as K V.
[02:51] Leila: so if we have the same system instruction for many requests, prefix caching should cut compute significantly?
[02:54] Maya: yes — in our tests prefix caching reduced token compute by ~20-40% depending on prefix length and reuse rate. for your workload, if system prompt is ~80 tokens and is present on 70% of requests, you'll see decent savings.
[03:09] [03:09] Aaron: i'll walk through the cost model we brought. spreadsheet link: (shared) "Redwood - batching_cache_cost_model_v1.xlsx"
[03:18] Aaron: model assumptions: model = 3B, quantized to 4-bit, KV cache enabled/disabled scenarios, batch sizes 1,4,8,16, dynamic batching windows 25/50/100ms; baseline GPU price assumptions reflect dedicated pool cost.
[03:34] Maya: note on quantization: going 4-bit yields ~2-3x speedup on some kernels, but not all ops benefit equally. runtime will pick quant kernels when safe.
[03:42] [03:42] Raj: can you show a concrete example? like if we enable prefix caching and batch size 8, what happens to cost/latency?
[03:49] Maya: sure. from the sheet, for a 3B at seq256, batch8 with prefix cache on, the per-1k-token GPU cost drops by about 38% and p95 latency for median requests stayed ~320ms, but cold (no cache) first-request p95 was ~520ms.
[04:05] Leila: that cold start penalty is worrying for interactive UI flows. can you mitigate it?
[04:09] Maya: options: pre-warm pools with pinned warm workers, serve system prompt from warm cache or keep a tiny pool of warm instances for latency-sensitive routes. Redwood supports route-level policies that keep min warm capacity.
[04:20] [04:20] Evan: how does this interact with autoscaling? we don't want to pay for idle GPUs 24/7.
[04:25] Aaron: recommended pattern: small hot pool for low p95 targets (1-2 GPUs), then autoscale additional capacity for throughput. you can set burst policies to use burst capacity only during business hours. those settings are part of Dedicated config.
[04:38] Aaron: also important — model variant fallback: if dedicated capacity is exhausted we can route to hosted model variant (slower/cheaper) so your app stays online.
[04:47] Raj: what's the expected cost delta hosted vs dedicated?
[04:50] Maya: depends but roughly hosted might be ~1.5-2x per-token because of multi-tenant and margin; dedicated is more efficient at scale. sheet has numbers per 1M tokens scenario.
[04:59] [04:59] Maya: next, we show how Redwood Optimize suggests batch sizes automatically based on your trace distribution. here's an example trace ingest we ran for a customer. it looks at arrival intervals, seq length distribution, and reuse fraction for prefixes.
[05:15] Maya: (screen share) this histogram shows a heavy tail in seq length — that matters because large seqs reduce effective batching density.
[05:22] Leila: our seqs vary; summaries can be 512 tokens sometimes, full notes 2048 for batch archive jobs.
[05:29] Maya: then you'd want to separate workloads: interactive short seq route with low batch/window and long async summarization job with very large batch and separate dedicated pool or job queue.
[05:40] Raj: can you quantify savings if we split interactive vs async?
[05:43] Maya: in our back-of-envelope: if 60% of tokens can be moved to async huge batches, you can cut overall cluster cost by ~35% while keeping interactive p95 within SLO.
[05:55] [05:55] Sasha: procurement question — will any of these optimizations affect data residency or compliance? i.e., caching means state; is that logged and encrypted?
[06:03] Aaron: good point. prefix/KV caches are treated as ephemeral storage; by default we encrypt at rest and you can opt to store cache in customer-managed KMS or disable persistent caching. we'll send SOC2 and encryption docs.
[06:17] Maya: also logs: access to cache keys and evictions are auditable in the console. We can show that in the security doc we share.
[06:26] [06:26] Evan: thought about eviction policies — how do you prevent cache poisoning if clients send weird prefixes?
[06:30] Maya: we hash and sign prefix keys and apply size/age-based eviction, plus per-tenant quotas. there are also TTLs and canary policies.
[06:39] Raj: can you run a benchmark with our traces to prove the cost numbers?
[06:42] Aaron: yes, that was the plan for the POC; we want Leila to share anonymized traces and we'll run a 1-week dedicated benchmark against your QPS targets with agreed metrics.
[06:51] [06:51] Maya: quick demo: console view — Optimize suggestions page. it shows recommended batch size with expected cost delta and estimated p95 impact. you can accept suggestions and promote them to runtime config.
[07:04] Maya: here's an example suggestion: for route /summarize-short use dynamic batching window=50ms, max batch=8, and enable prefix_cache for system prompt with TTL 12h. expected cost delta -26% and p95 change +12% (i.e., slightly higher but within SLO).
[07:19] [07:19] Leila: will enabling prefix cache increase memory footprint on GPU?
[07:22] Maya: some memory overhead for local KV storage per worker but much less than full activations; persistent cache can be offloaded to remote store if needed. memory footprint numbers are in the spreadsheet.
[07:33] Aaron: let's talk about the cost model assumptions so Nimbus knows where variance can come from: model size, quantization effectiveness, GPU type, kernel coverage, cache hit rate, and request arrival distribution are the big ones.
[07:45] Maya: and specifically kernel coverage — some attention ops don't speed up on low-bit quantization or certain hardware. Optimize flags these cases.
[07:53] [07:53] Raj: any quick wins for us in the first two weeks?
[07:56] Aaron: yes: 1) enable lightweight prefix caching for the most common system prompt, 2) introduce a small hot pool (1-2 GPUs) with dynamic batching window 25-50ms for interactive route, 3) route large async jobs to a separate job queue with large batch sizes. those are low effort and high ROI.
[08:13] Leila: timeline for implementing prefix caching in our code? it's mostly a runtime switch?
[08:18] Maya: for Redwood-hosted or dedicated customers, it's a config toggle plus a small integration to sign prefix keys; our SDKs have helpers. we'll provide code snippets.
[08:29] [08:29] Aaron: showing Excel sheet again — here's scenario A (no cache) cost per 1M tokens = $X; scenario B (prefix cache + batch8) cost per 1M tokens = $X*0.62. we've anonymized numbers in the shared sheet.
[08:45] Raj: any risk of quality regression with caching? like stale prefixes or changed system instruction?
[08:49] Maya: we version prefix keys. when you update system prompt we bump the prefix signature so old cache entries are invalidated. you can also keep a rolling TTL to avoid staleness.
[08:58] [08:58] Maya: moving on to the Optimize flow for canary rollouts — you can A/B different batch/quant configs and we measure response quality via evals. it's integrated with the eval hooks in Redwood Console.
[09:11] Leila: great — can we plug in our unit tests/eval harness?
[09:14] Maya: yes, we have an API to push eval sets and threshold alerts.
[09:19] [09:19] Raj: procurement — cost predictability is important for budgeting. do you have rate cards or just usage invoices?
[09:24] Aaron: we do usage-based billing for hosted; Dedicated is commit-based with monthly/annual reserved capacity. for POC we can do a short-term reserved dev pool to get predictable numbers.
[09:36] Sasha: will you provide a POC price estimate?
[09:38] Aaron: yes we'll send a POC estimate in the next email based on the shared spreadsheet numbers and expected QPS.
[09:45] [09:45] Maya: some gotchas: if your request distribution has a high fraction of unique prefixes, prefix caching benefit is diminished. Optimize will compute an expected hit-rate from traces and show ROI.
[09:56] Leila: okay let's talk about the benchmark mechanics. how do you handle sensitive PHI tokens in traces?
[10:01] Aaron: please anonymize PII before upload; if needed we can run the benchmark in your VPC or Private deployment so traces never leave your network. we also support customer-managed KMS for any stored artifacts.
[10:15] [10:15] Evan: for on-prem or VPC POCs, what's the minimum infra footprint?
[10:19] Maya: for a 3B-style benchmark you'd need at least 1-2 GPUs for warm worker pool and additional for throughput; we have a sizing guide we'll share.
[10:30] Raj: can we review the suggested runtime config now?
[10:33] Maya: yes — (shared) route configs: /summarize-interactive: dynamic batch window 50ms, max batch 8, prefix_cache_on=true, min_warm_capacity=1; /summarize-async: batch window 500ms, max batch 64, persistent_kv_offload=true.
[10:55] [10:55] Leila: what's persistent_kv_offload?
[10:56] Maya: offloading the persistent KV to an external store (like Redis or s3-backed object store) to reduce GPU memory pressure. Redwood manages eviction and warm-up.
[11:05] Raj: does that add network overhead that will impact latency?
[11:08] Maya: small impact for cold misses, but warm hits are cached in worker local mem. for cold misses there's extra ms, but it's amortized across long prefixes.
[11:19] [11:19] Aaron: i want to flag the observability piece — the console shows token-level cost, hit rates on prefix cache, and a per-route breakdown; that will help you iterate.
[11:29] Sasha: procurement will need the security pack. can you confirm SOC2 + encryption details?
[11:33] Aaron: yes, we'll attach SOC2, ISO snippet, KMS options and eviction/audit logs in the follow-up.
[11:40] [11:40] Maya: quick QA from me: any constraints on network egress or private registry we should know?
[11:44] Evan: we route to a private registry and have strict egress rules; we'll provide the network diagram.
[11:49] Leila: last technical Q: how do you measure cache hit rate in the console?
[11:52] Maya: metric is prefix_hit_count / prefix_lookup_total per route, with sample traces showing examples of hits/misses.
[11:59] [11:59] Raj: ok, sounds good. next steps recap?
[12:02] Aaron: recap: Aaron to share spreadsheet and POC estimate; Maya to share runtime config snippets and canary notes; Leila to share traces; Evan to share infra constraints. schedule POC week starting 2025-08-04.
[12:15] Leila: thanks. this was helpful.
[12:17] Aaron: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the files.
[12:21] [12:21] End of meeting

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions of acronyms (K V cache vs KV cache), speaker attribution generic at times. Some timestamps approximate.
